name: Render
tagline: Deploy one containerized web service with automatic TLS and health checks

pricing.notes: Official Starter web-service monthly price; other resources cost extra.

tiers.name: Hobby workspace
tiers.limits: 1 member; unlimited projects; 2 environments/project; 25 services; 5 GB outbound bandwidth; 500 build minutes/month
tiers.notes: Workspace fee only; service compute is billed separately.

tiers.name: Pro workspace
tiers.limits: Unlimited members; 25 GB outbound bandwidth; 15 custom domains; 1,000 build minutes/month
tiers.notes: Flat workspace fee; service compute is billed separately.

tiers.name: Scale workspace
tiers.limits: Unlimited members; 1 TB outbound bandwidth; 25 custom domains; 5,000 build minutes/month
tiers.notes: Includes organization controls, SSO/SCIM and advanced RBAC; compute is separate.

tiers.notes: Price is per service instance; horizontal scaling multiplies the charge.

tiers.name: Web service, Standard compute

tiers.name: Web service, Pro compute
tiers.limits: 4 GB RAM; 2 CPU per running instance

tiers.name: Web service, Pro Plus compute
tiers.limits: 8 GB RAM; 4 CPU per running instance

tiers.name: Web service, Pro Max compute

pricing.freeTierCaps: Hobby workspace: 1 member, 25 services, 5 GB outbound bandwidth and 500 build minutes/month; Free web-service compute supplies 750 instance-hours/workspace/month and spins down after 15 idle minutes
pricing.billingTerms: monthly only; no annual workspace or compute plan shown; compute is charged per running instance
pricing.hiddenCosts: Workspace fee and compute stack: each scaled instance is billed separately; outbound bandwidth is $0.15/GB over plan, extra custom domains are $0.25/domain/month, extra build capacity is $5/1,000 minutes on Pro/Scale, persistent disks and databases cost extra

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Render, deploy one containerized web service with automatic TLS and health checks. The hard boundary is managed runtime, databases, private networking, builds, scaling, and support, plus infrastructure scale, operations, and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Deploy one containerized web service on a user-owned server with automatic TLS and health checks, route domains, retain logs, and perform backups.
whatYouLose: managed runtime, databases, private networking, builds, scaling, and support
ongoingBurden: patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Render because hosting products sell an operations team and failure-domain diversity, not merely a deploy button. The recurring cost buys patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Coolify
priorArt.desc: Active open-source self-hosting platform for applications, databases, and services.

alternatives.name: Coolify
alternatives.desc: One container, automatic TLS, health checks, logs, and restarts on hardware you pay for directly.

facts.install: Coolify Cloud signup or one-line install script on a fresh Linux server
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted control data is in an internal PostgreSQL container; deployed apps and databases remain in Docker containers, volumes, and configuration on the user's servers
facts.gapVsPaid: Coolify can provide TLS, health checks, logs, and restarts, but it does not give you Render's fully managed host fleet, availability engineering, autoscaling, or support.
facts.setupBlocker: A VPS with root SSH access, open ports, DNS, and responsibility for server patching and application-data backups

alternatives.name: Dokku
alternatives.desc: The original tiny Heroku-on-one-box; excellent once you are comfortable treating a server like a pet.

facts.install: Bootstrap script on a fresh supported Ubuntu or Debian VM, then add an SSH key and domain
facts.dataFormat: Application images, configuration, logs, and persistent Docker volumes live on the user's server; service data lives in installed database-plugin volumes
facts.gapVsPaid: Dokku deploys a containerized web service cleanly, but automatic health recovery stops at the server you operate and there is no managed platform underneath it.
facts.setupBlocker: A fresh Linux VM, sudo/SSH competence, DNS, and command-line-only administration

alternatives.name: Dokploy
alternatives.desc: A newer self-hosted PaaS for apps and databases, with previews, TLS, logs, and backups in the same control plane.

facts.install: Dokploy Cloud signup or one-line install script on a Linux VPS
facts.dataFormat: Dokploy metadata is stored in PostgreSQL; application and database data lives in Docker named volumes or bind mounts on the deployment servers, with optional S3 backups
facts.gapVsPaid: Dokploy supplies TLS, logs, previews, and backups, but you still own the host, networking, capacity, patching, and high availability that Render manages.
facts.setupBlocker: A VPS with at least 2 GB RAM, free ports 80/443/3000, DNS, and ongoing Docker/server administration

rejectedAlternatives.name: Render Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Free web services spin down, lose local files, and are for hobby or testing workloads, not a durable Render replacement.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Starter Web Service plan and a single-server personal platform DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Render in an empty repository.
Use Docker Compose, Caddy, PostgreSQL, Redis, and a small Go control plane; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: deploy one containerized web service on a user-owned server with automatic TLS and health checks, route domains, retain logs, and perform backups.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Accept a Git repository or container image and one explicit Dockerfile-based build path.
Implement applications, environments, secrets, domains, health checks, and rolling container replacement.
Use Caddy for automatic TLS and route only to healthy local containers.
Capture bounded build and runtime logs and expose restart, rollback, and redeploy actions.
Back up PostgreSQL metadata and document backups for each deployed application's data volumes.
Add host metrics, disk alerts, update instructions, disaster recovery, and a prominent single-server warning.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out multi-region or serverless infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out managed data stores and global edge delivery.
Deliberately leave out DDoS response, compliance, and guaranteed uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
